claims.text: The initial nanoparticles are equiatomic MnFeCoNiCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Rapid colloidal synthesis produces an initially homogeneous solid-solution phase in these nanoparticles.
Defective T-graphite has defect-mediated nanoparticle anchoring sites.
Defective T-graphite provides stronger nanoparticle–support interfacial bonding than conventional inert carbon.
Stronger defect-mediated anchoring reduces nanoparticle migration during high-temperature exposure.
Stronger defect-mediated anchoring reduces nanoparticle coarsening and sintering during high-temperature exposure.
Stronger defect-mediated anchoring reduces elemental segregation during high-temperature exposure.
Reduced migration, coarsening, and segregation preserve the near-equiatomic solid-solution state.
Preservation of the near-equiatomic solid-solution state is critical to retaining catalytic performance.
Preservation of the near-equiatomic solid-solution state is critical to retaining thermoelectric performance.
Relative to inert carbon, defective T-graphite will yield less nanoparticle sintering under the stated conditions.
Relative to inert carbon, defective T-graphite will yield less elemental segregation under the stated conditions.
Relative to inert carbon, defective T-graphite will provide superior retention of catalytic performance.
Relative to inert carbon, defective T-graphite will provide superior retention of thermoelectric performance.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to colloidally synthesized equiatomic HEA nanoparticles under reducing or inert atmospheres.
Applicability under fully oxidizing conditions, substantially different compositions, or other support materials is undetermined.
The improvement from support interactions may be modest relative to intrinsic high-temperature diffusion effects.
